extracted.intended_audience: researchers and grant writers preparing Specific Aims pages (e.g., NIH/other agency applicants; early-stage investigators and mentors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting the one-page Specific Aims section of a grant proposal: how to structure the page (intro, rationale, aims, impact), what content to include, formatting and writing-style recommendations, and common do's/don'ts for persuading review panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience: write to an educated non-expert reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: The Aims page should be written to an educated non-expert audience, giving a basic understanding of the problem while providing just enough detail to indicate mastery for expert reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save field-specific details, depth of expertise, and extensive pilot data for later sections; keep content 'need to know' only. Aim to engage reviewers who may have different backgrounds so they can become advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening sentence: compelling, specific, and predictive
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 1 should begin with a first sentence that is compelling, catchy, includes all pertinent key words, and conveys importance and impact so that the rest of the paragraph is predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly broad openers (e.g., 'Heart disease is the number one cause of death'). Prefer a sentence that states the condition, why it’s important, and hints at the proposed solution. Example: instead of broad neurologic diseases, focus on thrombolysis in stroke and its impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce problem, knowledge gap, and alignment with funder mission
rubrics_metrics.description: End the introductory paragraph by educating the reviewer on important existing knowledge, identifying the knowledge gap or critical need, and relating the project to the funding agency’s mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear phrases like 'these studies were limited by...', 'no one knows why...', or 'a gap remains...'. If applicable, use terminology from the funding announcement to show alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief background: summarize known information concisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide one or two high-level sentences summarizing important existing knowledge to ground the proposal without becoming esoteric or lengthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize citations on the Aims page because they can distract and belong in the background section. Balance enough detail to orient the reviewer but avoid jargon and excessive depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge major controversies briefly
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly note major controversies that might challenge the proposal so reviewers are reassured and continue reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve controversies here; just allay concerns so the reviewer is not diverted from the proposal's rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: present the solution and why now/why you
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 2 should describe the rationale: a high-level proposal to fill the identified gap, why it is the right solution at this time, and why this team is the right one to do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include succinct justification for the chosen approach, relevant qualifications or unique opportunities (e.g., novel resources, compelling pilot data), and an overall study objective or long-term goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective and hypothesis: realistic, achievable, and properly framed
rubrics_metrics.description: State an overall study objective that is realistic and achievable and link it to a central hypothesis or statement of need. Take care that the objective is not phrased simply as 'to test a hypothesis' but as what will be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grandiose objectives (e.g., 'cure cancer'); ensure the objective would advance the field regardless of outcome. Prepare a plan for interpreting and reporting negative or null findings (to be explained in later sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a 'burning platform' or urgency when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, explain why the study is urgent or timely (e.g., policy decisions depend on results, a critical path in the field), to emphasize prioritization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe why the work must be done now and what will be possible after the study is completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Aims: clarity, specificity, and no first mentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aims should be clear, achievable, directly related to prior paragraphs, conceptual rather than descriptive, and contain no new terms or 'first mentions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each aim should have a clear purpose and avoid redundant modifiers (e.g., 'in older male patients with prostate cancer'). Consistency with the central hypothesis and overall project goal is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb choice in aims: use active, specific action verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concise action verbs (e.g., 'measure') rather than vague or descriptive verbs (e.g., 'correlate', 'describe', 'explore', 'investigate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on agency expectations, aims may be phrased as incomplete sentences starting with action words. Prefer verbs that imply an achievable outcome rather than exploratory phrasing (e.g., 'measure' vs 'determine whether').

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and scope of aims: 2–4 aims, three preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Two to four aims are acceptable; three is generally 'just right'. Number and scope should reflect study duration and budget: fewer aims for small/short grants, more for larger program grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims define the scope of work and can make a study seem too ambitious if excessive. Pilot studies may have fewer aims. Avoid proposing exploratory aims that appear weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid aim dependency (aim independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aims should be related but not dependent on the success of another aim; avoid creating a chain where failure of one aim cripples others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies to avoid dependency include using separate populations, different approaches, or designing aims that yield interpretable results even if a prior aim fails (e.g., test multiple assays rather than rely on one new assay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub-aims: use sparingly due to complexity and criticism risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Sub-aims (1a, 1b, etc.) can organize experiments under a single aim but increase complexity and opportunities for reviewer criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits of organization against potential for confusion; include sub-aims only when they clearly add clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include testable hypotheses, approaches, and alternatives as appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where expected by the agency, state hypotheses and brief experimental/analytic approaches for each aim, plus anticipated challenges and proposed solutions or alternative approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each aim has a clear link to methods or planned interpretation; include alternative approaches so the study can succeed even if initial plans fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Impact paragraph: state innovation, payoff, and next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The closing paragraph should outline expected outcomes, highlight innovation and impact for the agency/field/society, and suggest specific next studies or career impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close the loop back to the opening sentence, be specific about value/return on investment, and describe what the project will enable next (including who the investigator will become if career development is involved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting: follow agency rules; maximize readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting (bolding, underlining, fonts, margins) is often dictated by the funding agency; keep reader comfort in mind by maximizing white space and readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write full Aims Page in 12-point font and one-inch margins before reformatting; use left justification (recommended), be judicious with emphasis (save one style for resubmissions), and follow any agency-specific font/spacing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure use: include simple conceptual figures when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider adding a simple figure (conceptual model or key-variable relationships) to save words and reinforce the story visually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep figures simple; when added, consider wrapping text and placing figures where they support left-justified text. Figures should clarify the narrative, not add complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing style: clarity, concision, active voice, and storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize clarity and concision (short words, delete unnecessary phrases), use active verbs and first person when appropriate, and employ a journalistic/topic-sentence style with storytelling elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use topic sentence then supporting material; storytelling (including a composite clinical case for clinical/translational proposals) can make the rationale memorable. Use passive voice sparingly and only where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize citations on the Specific Aims page
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations are normally minimized because they can distract reviewers and will be included in the background section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If citations are necessary, keep them minimal and only when they materially affect understanding of the problem or gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do's and Don'ts (practical checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice do's (write aims early, use active verbs, consider a figure, write to non-experts) and don'ts (don't state an untestable hypothesis, avoid vague jargon, don't propose a fishing expedition, avoid overly descriptive verbs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly: DO write aims early and revise; DO use active verbs and massive parallelism; DO consider a figure; DO write to non-experts. DON'T state a hypothesis you cannot test; DON'T use 'correlate/describe/explore/investigate' as primary aim verbs; DON'T propose a fishing expedition; DON'T use vague words and jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative assessment checklist (Table 4 items)
rubrics_metrics.description: A compact formative checklist to evaluate an Aims page: Defining the Problem (what's known, gaps, problem to solve, urgency); Proposed Solution/Rationale (central hypothesis, why this study, team's qualifications); Specific Aims (variables linked to gaps, testable hypotheses and planned interpretations, alternative approaches); Payoff (expected outcome, innovation/impact, next logical study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these items to self-assess or peer-assess Aims pages during workshops or review; ensure each bullet is addressed succinctly on the Aims page or clearly reserved for later sections when appropriate.
